title: Harnessing gasotransmitters for orthopaedic infection therapy: Mechanisms and advanced delivery platforms
abstract: Orthopaedic infections are increasingly prevalent in the aging population, posing a significant clinical and economic burden. Despite progress in antimicrobial therapies, challenges such as antibiotic resistance and superbug emergence persist. Gas therapy has emerged as a promising strategy for managing orthopaedic infections. Classical gasotransmitters-including nitric oxide (NO), carbon monoxide (CO), and hydrogen sulfide (HS)-exhibit antibacterial and immunomodulatory effects at controlled concentrations, though improper dosing may induce adverse effects. This review critically examines the dual mechanisms through which gasotransmitters combat infection while promoting orthopaedic regeneration. We also survey advanced delivery platforms-such as smart scaffolds, nano-reservoirs, and on-demand release systems-engineered for targeted gasotransmitter delivery to infected bone tissue. Finally, we discuss current limitations and future prospects, aiming to inspire novel biomaterial designs for targeted therapeutic delivery and to advance gas therapy as a viable option for orthopaedic infection treatment.

title: Bioprinted core-shell living material platform for spatially controlled encapsulation of Bacillus subtilis and sustained metabolite exchange
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) represents an escalating global health crisis, demanding alternative strategies to reduce resistant pathogen burden across environments. Microbe-based biocontrol is promising, yet effectively deploying it in practical settings remains challenging. In this study, we present a 3D bioprinted core-shell construct featuring a polyethylene glycol diacrylate (PEGDA) shell with tunable nanoscale porosity, encapsulating germinable spores of the biocontrol agentTH035. This configuration supports long-term spore viability while providing protection from common environmental stressors including UV-C irradiation, ethanol exposure, and desiccation over 4 weeks. The nanoporous PEGDA shell enables effective bacterial confinement while facilitating sufficient metabolite exchange forgermination and growth, as well as suppression of methicillin-resistant(MRSA) growth by approximately one order of magnitude. This approach demonstrates the feasibility of embeddingspores within engineered scaffolds for extended competitive functionality. The versatility and scalability of digital light processing (DLP) based bioprinting offers significant potential for tailored designs and high-throughput manufacturing. This proof-of-concept platform may find future applications in areas such as biomedical packaging, environmental sanitation, and built environment surface coatings, particularly in settings where intermittent moisture or nutrient availability can support spore germination and biocontrol activity.

title: Artificial intelligence catalyzes antimicrobial peptide design
abstract: With broad-spectrum, low resistance, and multifunctional properties, antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) are promising therapeutic agents against drug-resistant pathogens, yet their discovery and optimization still remain challenging due to the complexity of sequence-function associations. Artificial intelligence (AI), through the construction of comprehensive data-driven models that assisted with miscellaneous learning strategies, enables de novo peptide design by learning latent representations inherent in peptide sequences as well as their biological properties to ensure physically plausible and biologically relevant predictions. Consequently, this paradigm enhances the likelihood of designing peptide candidates with significantly improved therapeutic potential, reducing resource-intensive trial-and-error processes and revealing the transformative impact of computational innovation in advancing next-generation therapeutics. Here, we provide a snapshot of this field and survey two modes of AI-driven technologies for AMP design, one concentrated on identifying whether current data possess antimicrobial activity (identification-oriented) and the other on generating AMP candidates with potential therapeutic properties (generation-oriented). We also highlight the challenges and limitations that still hinder AMP development even accelerated by AI, as well as the foreseeable prospects, from finer-grained explorations to model-driven data enrichment and model enhancement.

title: Antifungal mechanisms of volatile organic compounds and lactic acid produced by Lactiplantibacillus pentosus and their biocontrol application in fresh corn against Fusarium graminearum
abstract: Fusarium graminearum causes cereal spoilage and mycotoxin production. Currently, biocontrol microorganisms have emerged as a safe and promising strategy to manage the contamination of toxin-producing fungi in cereal grains. The primary objective was to elucidate the antifungal mechanism of an isolated strain of Lactiplantibacillus pentosus Q11 against F. graminearum and to evaluate the preservative effects of its cell-free supernatant (CFS) in fresh sweet corn. In vitro antifungal assays of L. pentosus Q11 showed strong antagonistic activity against F. graminearum, Aspergillus flavus, and Penicillium expansum, as well as the ability to reduce zearalenone. Moreover, whole-genome analysis revealed no genes related to virulence and antimicrobial resistance, and no hemolytic activity was observed, which suggested the potential safety of strain Q11. Moreover, the CFS of L. pentosus Q11 effectively inhibited the mycelial growth of F. graminearum, disrupted hyphal integrity, and induced fungal cell death. Moreover, 3 organic acids and 38 volatile compounds in the CFS of Q11 strain were identified by SPME-GC-MS and HPLC, in which 2-nonanone, 2-methylpyrazine, lactic acid, acetic acid were predominant compounds. The CFS and lactic acid combined with 2-nonanone severely damaged hyphae of F. graminearum, by disrupting cell membrane and wall, leading to leakage of intracellular substances, showing a synergistic antifungal effect of the two vital compounds. Subsequently, the treatments of CFS and combined agents significantly decreased 88.05% - 89.52% of fungal populations, and AFBand DON mycotoxin accumulation in fresh sweet corn after 12 days of storage compared to the control. The malondialdehyde content in the treated corn was decreased by 29.25% - 31.50%, consistent with the higher activities of POD and APX, thereby preserving their sensory attributes and nutritional quality. Metabolomic analysis revealed that L-glutamate, γ-glutamylcysteine, and oxidized glutathione were significantly downregulated in the glutathione metabolism pathway in the treated corn, indicating that CFS containing lactic acid and 2-nonanone could repress fungal growth and alleviate oxidative stress in fresh sweet corn. Overall, these findings demonstrate that L. pentosus Q11 with synergistic volatile organic compounds and lactic acid is a promising biocontrol agent in preserving fresh sweet corn.

title: The impact of prophylactic azithromycin on the developing preterm gut microbiome and resistome
abstract: Early-life antibiotic exposure can profoundly impact the developing preterm gut microbiome and resistome, with short- and long-term consequences for health. In a large multi-center ( = 28) study of 693 preterm infants, we investigated the effects of 10 d of prophylactic intravenous azithromycin on the gut microbiome and antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs). The AZithromycin ThErapy for Chronic Lung Disease of Prematurity (AZTEC) study was a double blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial of preterm infants (born < 30 weeks of gestation), treated from birth for 10 d with either intravenous azithromycin or placebo, and sampled longitudinally for 21 d or discharge. Using 16S rRNA gene sequencing, antibiotic susceptibility testing, and quantitative PCR, we show azithromycin reduced microbial diversity and the relative abundance of health-associatedand increased relative abundances of pathobiontsand. This early azithromycin treatment increased the number of macrolide-resistant genes, including the presence of(C), which persisted for the duration of the study. Probiotic use (at individual unit discretion) increased alpha diversity andrelative abundance, but did not fully mitigate the effects of azithromycin receipt. Combined azithromycin and probiotics further increased the enrichment ofand total ARGs, including(C). These findings highlight the impacts of antibiotic and probiotic use, both important in balancing infection control issues and microbiome disruption and antimicrobial resistance.

title: Modulation of the gut microbiome and resistome by antibiotic use, but not by subsequent 2'-fucosyllactose intake, in adults with overweight or obesity
abstract: Antibiotics are widely used to treat bacterial infections, yet overuse and misuse causes disruption of the gut microbiome and spread of antibiotic-resistant bacteria. Presence of antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) could be a determinant of the response to antibiotics. Supplementation with prebiotics may limit the detrimental antibiotic-induced effects on the microbiome, but whether this results in changes in the gut resistome is unclear. This study investigated the impact of eight-week 2'-fucosyllactose (2'-FL) supplementation after seven-day vancomycin use in 18 adults with overweight/obesity, a subset from a double-blind placebo-controlled randomized intervention. Whole-metagenome shotgun sequencing was used to characterize the gut microbiome and resistome at baseline, after vancomycin use and after supplementation. Seven-day vancomycin use disrupted microbial richness and diversity ( < 0.001) and changed microbial composition. No improvements in microbial recovery were detected after eight week 2'-FL supplementation compared to placebo. Resistome richness and diversity were not affected by vancomycin use, although the presence of specific ARGs changed. No differential impact of 2'-FL supplementation on resistome richness, diversity and composition was detected. While vancomycin use disrupted the gut microbiome and affected the resistome, the detectable effects of 2'-FL supplementation were limited. Future research should investigate antibiotic- and prebiotic-induced changes in the gut resistome in more detail.

Photocatalytic degradation of ciprofloxacin in water using BiOCl/Bi(2)S(3) composite: Experimental and model-predicted kinetic evaluation
abstract: Pharmaceutical contaminants in wastewater pose a significant environmental and public health risks. The conventional treatment methods often used suffer from incomplete degradation, high costs, and limited applicability. To address these shortcomings, this study developed an efficient visible-light-driven photocatalytic degradation of pharmaceutical contaminants particularly antibiotics which contributes significantly to environmental pollution. A novel BiOCl/BiSphotocatalyst was synthesized through a facile one-step method to enhance charge separation and suppress electron-hole recombination. The research used ciprofloxacin antibiotic as a model pollutant. The innovative aspect of this work lies in tuning the BiOCl: BiSmole ratios (3:1, 5:1, 7:1) to identify the optimal configuration for maximum degradation efficiency under visible light and found that 5:1 BiOCl/BiSachieved 94% of ciprofloxacin (CIP) degradation within 50 min under 300 W visible irradiation. Systematic optimization of pH, catalyst dosage, and initial concentration was also studied. The degradation pathway was elucidated through intermediate analysis, while kinetic studies using both linear and nonlinear Langmuir-Hinshelwood models confirmed the enhanced reactivity. This study also integrates computational kinetic modeling with experimental data using polynomial fit and showed the nonlinear relationship of predicted and experimental kinetic constants with different initial concentration of CIP. The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1007/s40201-026-01008-9.

Staphylococcus aureus in bovine intramammary infections: A global systematic review and meta-analysis of prevalence and antimicrobial resistance patterns
abstract: ()is a globally pervasive and economically significant pathogen in bovine intramammary infections (IMIs) and is responsible for both clinical and subclinical mastitis. This study systematically investigated the global epidemiology offrom bovine IMIs, addressing antimicrobial resistance (AMR) amongthrough a meta-analysis. A total of 143 studies published between 2000 and 2025 were identified through comprehensive searches, which were based on predefined inclusion criteria. The data were systematically extracted, and the statistical analyses were performed in R (v4.5.2). The meta-analysis included 143 studies (145,457 samples), with a pooledprevalence of 24.78% and high heterogeneity (I = 99.51%). Subgroup analyses demonstrated significant heterogeneity in prevalence by study design, publication year, and region, with greater heterogeneity in cross-sectional studies (I>95%, < 0.001). Meta-regression identified sample size as a significant source of heterogeneity (β = -0.00002, = 0.02; R = 3.41%). The highest prevalence was reported in Cameroon (67%), Sri Lanka (64.3%), Indonesia (57%), and India (44%), with the lowest prevalence reported in Poland (0.7%), Taiwan (2.0%), Australia (5.5%), and New Zealand (5.3%). AMR was highest for doxycycline (70.7%), penicillin (65.2%), and ampicillin (62.8%); moderate to oxacillin (44.6%) and vancomycin (40.2%); and lowest for gentamicin (27.5%) and amikacin (18.3%). is highly prevalent in bovine IMIs worldwide, with marked regional heterogeneity and substantial resistance to commonly used antimicrobials, emphasizing the urgent need for targeted surveillance, prudent antimicrobial use, and improved mastitis control strategies at the global and regional levels.

N-acetylcysteine as an adjunct to antibiotics against bacterial biofilms: A systematic review of in vitro evidence
abstract: N-acetylcysteine (NAC) is investigated as an antibiotic adjunct, but acidity, formulation and experimental context complicate interpretation. We evaluated comparative in-vitro evidence while distinguishing biofilm prevention, established-biofilm treatment and resistance evolution. MEDLINE/PubMed, Embase, Scopus and Web of Science were searched through August 2026, with supplementary searching. Extraction distinguished NAC preparation and exposure pH, medium, hydrodynamics, NAC-alone controls, treatment intent and interaction methodology. Results were synthesized by experimental context, regimen, phase and endpoint without pooling or whole-study efficacy voting. Fifty-five studies were included: 7 evaluated combination exposure during formation only, 37 after establishment only, 9 both, and 2 resistance evolution. NAC-alone arms were documented in 39 studies, partial or formulation-specific in 9, and not identified in 7. Only two studies included a continuous-flow model. Selected combinations improved biofilm-associated outcomes, but intrinsic-acidic and neutralized preparations, biomass and viability endpoints, and planktonic versus biofilm interaction tests were not interchangeable. Liposomal and catheter-lock findings differed by dose matching, isolate and control set. Polymyxin findings varied with organism, resistance background, medium and exposure; rifampicin-alone and rifampicin-containing multidrug comparators addressed different questions. NAC is a context-dependent experimental adjunct, not an established class-wide antibiotic potentiator. The evidence does not support clinical antibiotic dose reduction or routine NAC combination therapy. Translation requires controlled final exposure pH, matched monotherapy and formulation controls, clinically relevant background regimens, viable-burden and regrowth outcomes, and resistance monitoring.

Combating antimicrobial resistance through multimodal data via artificial intelligence
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) poses a critical global health challenge, leading to substantial mortality and economic losses without science-based interventions. Conventional approaches to combating AMR have important limitations in addressing this escalating threat. Recent advances in AI, including deep learning, large language models, and protein language models, provide new opportunities to integrate multimodal data for AMR research. However, evidence remains uneven, with many approaches limited to computational benchmarking rather than real-world validation. Here, we critically review AI applications in AMR, focusing on rapid diagnosis, therapeutic discovery, and clinical decision support. AI-based diagnostic models can identify resistant pathogens and predict resistance profiles, but most lack prospective clinical evaluation. AI-assisted drug discovery and alternative therapies have generated promising candidates, although most remain at computational, in vitro, or early preclinical stages. Large language models may support decision-making, but their clinical use remains preliminary. Successful translation of AI into clinical and One Health practice will require representative datasets, independent validation, prospective evaluation, and robust governance.

abstract: Mastitis is a multifactorial disease with major consequences for production, animal welfare, and public health, yet it remains less studied in goats than in cows. Moreover, reports of antimicrobial resistance among bacteria isolated from mastitic goats are scarce. In Ethiopia, treatment decisions for mastitis largely rely on empirical clinical experience rather than routine antimicrobial susceptibility testing. To address this gap, a cross-sectional study was conducted from November to December 2024 in Waghimra, Amhara, Ethiopia, to identify the major bacterial causes of mastitis and to evaluate their antimicrobial susceptibility patterns. Bacterial isolation, identification, and antimicrobial susceptibility testing followed standard protocols, and statistical analyses were performed using Stata 17 and WHONET software. The overall goat-level mastitis prevalence was 24.69% (98/397), comprising 2.52% (10/397) clinical and 22.28% (88/395) subclinical mastitis.spp. (47/129; 36.43%) was the predominant isolate, followed by(12/129; 9.30%) andspp. (3/129; 2.33%). Strengthening One Health Antimicrobial Resistance Surveillance in Bangladesh: Insights from the Fleming fund country grant
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is an escalating global public health concern, with particularly severe implications for low and middle-income countries such as Bangladesh. In Bangladesh context, fragmented surveillance systems and the extensive use of antimicrobials across human, animal, and aquaculture sectors contribute to the rapid emergence and spread of resistance. Strengthening integrated surveillance through a One Health approach is therefore crucial to support effective policy development and response strategies. This review outlines the policy, implementation, and key outcomes of the Fleming Fund Country Grant in Bangladesh between 2020 and 2025. It draws upon multiple data sources, including programme reports, routine AMR surveillance data, laboratory capacity-building initiatives, and stakeholder engagement activities across human, animal, aquaculture, and environmental sectors. Through this initiative, a coordinated national AMR surveillance network was established, comprising 20 laboratories across multiple sectors, including three designated national reference laboratories. The initiative strengthened surveillance through the introduction of standardized protocols and SOPs, improved diagnostic capacity, skilled workforce, and implementation of laboratory quality assurance systems, including EQA and NEQA. These measures enhanced the accuracy, consistency, and reliability of AMR surveillance data. In addition, the establishment of a national AMR data integration platform facilitated real time data sharing and evidence-based decision-making. A total of 208,346 bacterial isolates were analyzed, with AST results reported to the AMR dashboard across the human, and animal, health sectors. Overall, the Fleming Fund programme has made a substantial contribution to strengthening integrated AMR surveillance in Bangladesh by operationalizing a One Health framework. Continued political commitment, increased domestic investment, and the institutionalization of surveillance systems will be essential to sustain these gains and ensure long-term resilience against AMR.

Microfluidic-assembled curcumin ionizable lipid nanoparticles enhance aqueous delivery and antibiofilm activity against Staphylococcus aureus
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance and biofilm-associated infections demand novel therapeutic strategies. Curcumin is a natural polyphenol with broad-spectrum antimicrobial activity; however, its clinical utility is fundamentally constrained by negligible aqueous solubility and limited biofilm penetration. Here, we used microfluidic assembly to prepare curcumin-loaded ionizable lipid nanoparticles (Cur@LNP) with three clinically established ionizable lipids (SM-102, MC-3, and ALC-0315). The resulting formulations were uniform, with hydrodynamic diameters of approximately 90 nm and polydispersity indices near 0.1. Relative to free curcumin in DMSO, Cur@LNP lowered the minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) 8-fold and the minimum bactericidal concentration (MBC) 16-fold against planktonic, and markedly reduced viable biofilm-resident cells at matched concentrations. Scanning electron microscopy showed that Cur@LNP treatment remodeled mature biofilms into irregular, debris-rich aggregates with reduced extracellular matrix coverage. Notably, antimicrobial performance was indistinguishable across the three structurally distinct ionizable lipids at every concentration tested. Within this in vitro, single-strain system, the antibiofilm effect is therefore dominated by the cargo (curcumin) rather than by ionizable-lipid chemistry, and it is most likely attributed to enhanced aqueous solubilization of curcumin rather than to engagement of the lipid headgroup with the biofilm matrix. These results position microfluidic-assembled ionizable LNPs as a reproducible, scalable solubilization platform for poorly water-soluble natural antimicrobials.

title: Metagenomic analysis of commensal small mammal samples from an international cargo shipping area, Bangkok Port, reveals potential zoonotic pathogens and implications for One Health surveillance
abstract: Commensal small mammals, such as rats and shrews, are recognized reservoirs for numerous zoonotic pathogens; however, their role in pathogen circulation at transport hubs remains underexplored. This study employs shotgun metagenomic sequencing to characterize microbial communities and assess zoonotic potential in tissue samples from commensal small mammals captured at Bangkok Port, an international cargo shipping hub in Thailand between June and August 2025. Following host read depletion, taxonomic profiling was performed to identify bacterial taxa of public health relevance, including sequences assigned tospp.,,, and. The virulence factor and antibiotic resistance gene profiles revealed that some of these pathogens have pathogenic potential and are related to drug-resistant bacteria. In addition,was identified as a shared taxon among rats, shrews, and their associated fleas. The findings support the ecological roles of mammalian hosts and their ectoparasites as reservoirs for pathogens of public health concern. These results emphasize the need to strengthen surveillance programs for commensal small mammals to monitor and mitigate the spread of transboundary pathogens at international maritime gateways.

Wild boar as a sentinel species for ecosystem health surveillance: A review
abstract: Sentinel surveillance uses selected species that are widely distributed, easily sampled, and exposed to multiple health threats as indicators of ecosystem health. The Eurasian wild boar () is a broadly distributed game species that meets these conditions. We conducted a systematic review to assess the suitability of the wild boar as a sentinel or indicator species for monitoring health hazards relevant to ecosystem health, focusing on the hazards monitored, methods, justification for use, perceived performance, limitations, and proposed improvements. We identified 86 studies explicitly framing the wild boar as a sentinel species, covering a wide range of hazards, including 30 pathogens, 44 environmental contaminants, two biological toxins and 13 antimicrobial resistance (AMR) indicators. It was used to monitor pathogens (57%), environmental contaminants (31.4%), AMR (12.8%), and biological toxins (3.5%). Research effort was concentrated in Europe (84.9%) and relied mostly on hunted animals (90.7%). Wild boar were frequently selected as sentinels due to their previous use as indicators of ecosystem health in the literature, omnivorous diet, wide distribution, and accessibility as game species. However, hunting-based sampling may introduce biases, while post-mortem conditions and ecological variability may affect results. Despite this, 74.4% of studies supported their use as sentinels, particularly for pathogens and environmental contaminants. In contrast, their perceived suitability for AMR was more variable, and no quality assessment was available for biological toxins. Overall, wild boar sentinel surveillance is considered logistically efficient and valuable for monitoring ecosystem health hazards. However, its effectiveness is context-dependent and influenced by methodological and ecological limitations. Improving surveillance design through systematic sampling, alternative sample sources (e.g., found-dead animals or non-invasive methods), integration of multi-species data, and inclusion of covariates could enhance the reliability of findings within a One Health framework.

title: Global spread of carbapenem-resistant Providencia driven by high-risk lineages and plasmid co-evolution
abstract: Carbapenem-resistant(CRP) is a formidable opportunistic pathogen with extensive drug resistance, posing an increasing threat to human, animal, and environmental health. However, its global genomic epidemiology and resistome-plasmidome co-evolution within a One Health context remain poorly understood. Here, we conducted a comprehensive population genomic and plasmid analysis of 1197 CRP isolates from 35 countries spanning 2012-2025. We reclassified the CRP population into ninespecies, identifyingandas established epidemic species alongside the rapid emergence ofand. We pinpointed 2019 as a critical inflection point, marking the transition from endemic stability to rapid global epidemic expansion (80.8% isolates in 2019-2025). Ten intercontinentally disseminated high-risk sequence types (e.g., ST46, ST79), each with strict species-ST specificity, were responsible for global spread. Thegene (62.4% prevalence) was the predominant carbapenem gene, exhibiting strong geographic and species specificity and mutual exclusion with other major carbapenem genes. Plasmids encoded approximately 80% of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) genes, with 78.0% of these plasmids belonging to 75 stable clusters. These clusters evolved a dual specialist-generalist strategy, with the broad-host-range cluster 72 mediating interspecies AMR transmission and cluster 7 acting as a super-vector carrying six carbapenem genes. Importantly, CRP circulated across interconnected human, animal, and environmental reservoirs, with distinct host-associated species distributions suggesting ecological niche adaptation and potential cross-host dissemination of resistance determinants. These findings demonstrate that the global expansion of CRP is driven by the combined evolution of high-risk clones and mobile genetic elements across interconnected ecological sectors, underscoring the need for integrated One Health surveillance and coordinated interventions spanning clinical, veterinary, agricultural, and environmental settings.

abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) has intensified in recent years, raising concerns about the potential impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on AMR dynamics. However, the influence of pandemic on the enviromental occurrence and dissemination of antibiotic-resistant genes (ARGs) remains under investigation. Wastewater-based epidemiology (WBE) provides an integrated view of community-level AMR dynamics, yet long-term assessments spanning the pandemic period remain limited. This study investigated the occurrence, temporal patterns, and seasonal behavior of two clinically relevant carbapenemase genes,and, in raw wastewater from the Attica region over a five-year period (July 2021-September 2025). A sensitive and specific 3-plex qPCR assay was developed and analytically validated for the simultaneous quantification of,, and 16S rRNA, the latter serving as a stable bacterial load indicator. Across the monitoring period,was consistently detected, showing a steady increase and reaching its highest concentrations in 2023, whileexhibited intermittent but pronounced surges, particularly in 2023. Comparison with community SARS-CoV-2 viral loads suggest temporal association with AMR signatures in wastewater. Seasonal analysis showed non-uniform patterns, with atypical warm-season peaks of both ARGs in 2023-2024 and a return to classical autumn-winter peaks in 2025, suggesting a gradual restoration of pre-pandemic seasonality. To our knowledge, this is among the first long-term WBE studies to characterize post-COVID-19 shifts in ARG occurrence and seasonality. The results demonstrate that the pandemic period was associated with elevated and fluctuating ARG levels in the urban wastewater system, emphasizing the need for sustained AMR monitoring. These findings address critical knowledge gaps in environmental AMR surveillance and support the integration of WBE into public health strategies aimed at mitigating AMR dissemination.

Genomic epidemiology to investigate the origins and zoonotic implications of antibiotic-resistant Escherichia coli on beef and lamb meat sold by independent butchers in Wales
abstract: Many studies have identified antibiotic resistant (ABR)on meat. Appropriate hand hygiene and cooking practices should minimize the risk of gastrointestinal colonisation with ABRfound on meat, and the subsequent chance of causing resistant opportunistic extraintestinal infection. There are large gaps in our understanding of the prevalence, origins and zoonotic potential of ABRfound on meat, however, and particularly for meat reared in extensive farming systems. Wales is a devolved nation within the United Kingdom having large populations of extensively-reared sheep and beef cattle. To help address knowledge gaps around ABRon extensively reared meat, therefore, beef mince and lamb loin/leg steaks/chops were purchased from 50 (beef) and 46 (lamb) independent butchers across Wales. Following enrichment culture, 200 g meat samples were found to be positive forresistant to amoxicillin (31% positivity), streptomycin (28%), spectinomycin (29%), amoxicillin-clavulanate (11%), 3rd generation cephalosporins (2%) and fluoroquinolones (5%). Phylogenetic analysis confirmed that Welsh lamb meat ABRisolates ( = 78) are more closely related to those found in faecal samples collected around sheep ( = 352) than around beef cattle ( = 361) on Welsh farms. This suggests that faecal contamination at or around slaughter is their primary origin. We found no closely related meat/infection clones (<20 SNPs distant and the same antibiotic resistance genes) when comparing ABRfrom Welsh meat ( = 91) and those causing extraintestinal infections in people ( = 2387) in an English region bordering Wales. We conclude, therefore, that the wider zoonotic implications of finding ABRon beef and lamb meat sold at independent butchers in Wales are small, though a more geographically and temporarily contemporaneous survey is warranted to address this further.

Sewage surveillance for assessing clinical antibiotic resistance prevalence: Combining metagenomic and phenotypic data
abstract: Surveillance of antibiotic resistance in clinical isolates is a cornerstone for the management of bacterial infections but is limited in large parts of the world, often due to lack of resources. Sewage surveillance has been proposed as a promising, resource-efficient complement to the traditional surveillance approach based on samples from many individual patients. Both phenotypic data on resistance in sewage isolates and abundance of antibiotic resistance genes in sewage have been shown to correlate with resistance prevalence in clinical isolates. Here, we aimed to directly compare and combine an isolate-based and a gene-based sewage surveillance approach to evaluate what best can reflect clinical resistance rates. The two approaches, based on susceptibility testing of collectedisolates and metagenomic sequencing, respectively, were applied to municipal sewage samples collected in ten European countries. The data generated was related to available data on resistance to aminopenicillins, fluoroquinolones, third generation cephalosporins and aminoglycosides prevalence in clinicalisolates using beta regression models. None of the tested individual predictors were superior across all four investigated classes of antibiotics. For modelling of aminopenicillin resistance, a clearly higher Rvalue was obtained when isolate-based and gene-based data was combined as predictors, also after adjusting for the number of included variables. We conclude that there could be a value of including both isolate- and gene-based sewage data for predictions of resistance rates in clinical isolates, while emphasizing the value of linking predictors to specific species and classes of antibiotics.

title: Clonal diversity, virulence factors and antibiotic resistance genes of Enterococcus faecalis and Klebsiella pneumoniae from urban rats in Malaysia
abstract: Peridomestic rats serve as important carriers of zoonotic pathogens, including multidrug-resistant bacteria such asand. However, information on the clonal diversity, antibiotic resistance, and virulence of these pathogens in wild urban rats remains limited, particularly in tropical settings. This study investigatedandin urban rats from wet markets across four Malaysian states. A total of 277 rats (, = 177;, = 100) were trapped, and lung tissues were processed for bacterial isolation. Isolates were identified by 16S rDNA sequencing and examined for antibiotic susceptibility, resistance genes, and virulence factors using PCR. Clonal relationships were determined through multilocus sequence typing (MLST). Nineteenand sevenisolates were recovered. Allisolates carried multiple virulence factors (,,, and), and four tetracycline-resistant isolates possessed,, and. Five novelsequence types (ST730 - ST734) were identified. Allisolates carried the SHV gene; two also harbored FOX, and two possessedandvirulence factors. Two novelSTs (ST2641 and ST2642) were detected. Phylogenetic analyses revealed that both species displayed diverse sequence types scattered across global lineages. These findings suggest that urban rats may act as potential carriers of virulent and antibiotic-resistantand. These findings support the inclusion of urban rats in future One Health surveillance programs investigating antimicrobial resistance and virulent bacterial pathogens.

title: Virulence attenuation in ST11-K64 Klebsiella pneumoniae explains its divergent clinical manifestation from ST23-K1
Design, synthesis, and antibacterial activity study of pyrroloquinazoline diamine derivatives
Antimicrobial resistance patterns and polymicrobial co-detection characteristics of vaginal Group B Streptococcus in pregnant women: a retrospective study
Genetic determinants of hypervirulence with attenuated pathogenicity in a bla(NDM-1)-encoding Klebsiella pneumoniae causing neonatal sepsis
Copper-coated carbon nanotube surfaces for inhibiting biofilm formation by Staphylococcus aureus and Pseudomonas aeruginosa
abstract: Biofilm-associated infections caused by clinically important pathogens such as() and() remain a major challenge in healthcare settings due to enhanced antimicrobial resistance and persistence. In recent years, copper-coated carbon nanotubes (Cu-CNTs) have gained considerable attention as promising antimicrobial nanomaterials for preventing biofilm formation on medical devices and hospital-associated surfaces. This review summarizes recent advances in the development and application of Cu-CNT-based antimicrobial coatings, with an emphasis on their antibacterial and antibiofilm activities against Gram-positive and Gram-negative pathogens. The synergistic combination of the high surface-area-to-volume ratio of CNTs and the potent antimicrobial properties of copper (Cu) ions enhances microbial inhibition. Previous studies suggest that Cu-CNTs interfere with initial bacterial adhesion, inhibit biofilm maturation, and disrupt established biofilms through mechanisms involving oxidative stress generation, membrane destabilization, and cellular damage. Furthermore, the review discusses the physicochemical characteristics, antimicrobial mechanisms, biomedical applications, and potential challenges associated with Cu-CNT coatings, including toxicity and biocompatibility concerns. Overall, Cu-CNT-based coatings represent a promising strategy for developing durable antimicrobial surfaces to control chronic biofilm-associated infections and reduce healthcare-associated contamination.

Synergistic antibacterial activity and mechanism of arginine combined with florfenicol against Escherichia coli
Differential modulation of gentamicin antibacterial activity by vitamin B12 and vitamin D3 against Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria: an in vitro-in silico study
Microbiota-constrained bacterial density limits phage infection in the gut and allows persistence of susceptible cells
abstract: With the rise of antibiotic resistance, bacteriophage-based treatments against bacterial infections have regained momentum. However, phage therapy has so far shown only moderate success in complex environments like the mammalian gut, where phages are particularly promising tools for microbiome engineering and specific elimination of opportunistic pathogens. Here, we use different murine models of intestinal colonization to quantitatively assess the minimal population size of susceptiblecells that is required for phage replication in the gut (replication threshold). We found that the composition of the intestinal microbiota is a key factor shaping phage-bacteria interactions by restricting the carrying capacity of susceptible host cells. We further demonstrate that the replication threshold enables coexistence of susceptible and resistant bacteria in phage-treated mice, with implications for phage-based applications in complex environments like the gut.

title: Extraction of chondroitin sulfate from chicken cartilage by Bacillus velezensis 259 fermentation: whole-genome analysis and process optimization
abstract: This study used chicken cartilage as the raw material and employed microbial fermentation with259 (259) to extract chondroitin sulfate (CS). The CS extraction rate served as the primary evaluation index to investigate the effects of bacterial inoculation amount, cartilage addition amount, and fermentation time on extraction efficiency. First,259 was evaluated for its gelatinolytic and proteolytic activities and safety-related characteristics, followed by whole-genome analysis to investigate its genomic features and the presence of potential virulence and antimicrobial resistance genes. Subsequently, single-factor experiments and response surface optimization were conducted. A quadratic polynomial model was established using the Box-Behnken design, and response surface analysis was performed to determine the optimal process parameters for CS extraction from fermented chicken cartilage using259. The results showed that the optimal extraction conditions were 6.2% inoculation amount, 22.5% cartilage addition amount, 37 °C, 180 r/min and 20.8 h fermentation time. Under these conditions, the CS extraction rate reached 17.9%. In addition, UV and Raman spectroscopy further showed that the crude CS extract exhibited spectral characteristics similar to those of the CS-A and CS-C standards. These findings demonstrated the feasibility of using259 fermentation for CS extraction from chicken cartilage and provided optimized process parameters for this approach. The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1007/s13205-026-05101-6.

Acute Otitis Externa-Antimicrobial Resistance in the US and Canada: Phase III Study Outcomes
abstract: The goal of this investigation was to characterize the microbiological profile and antimicrobial susceptibility patterns of pathogens isolated from AOE patients of 2 vehicle-controlled Phase III clinical trials and evaluate pathogen eradication rates achieved with finafloxacin otic suspension. In vitro MIC comparisons to other fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin, ofloxacin) are reported as supplementary susceptibility data and do not reflect direct randomized clinical comparisons. A total of 2683 bacteria isolated from 1234 AOE patients enrolled in 2 Phase III clinical studies in the United States, Puerto Rico, and Canada were analyzed. Specimens were collected from the external ear of subjects with AOE. Species-level identification for each bacterial isolate recovered was obtained by combining phenotypic and genotypic data. End point minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) testing was performed using Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute recommended methods. 72.7% of the pre-therapy bacteria were Gram-positive and 27.3% Gram-negative. Most frequent bacterial isolates werespp. (46.7%) followed byspp. (19.5%). Methicillin resistance was detected in 17.0% of.(MRSA) and 33.2% of.(MRSE) isolates. Ciprofloxacin resistance was identified in 12.5% of.and 14.0% of.isolates. Finafloxacin eradicated 86.4% of the MRSA isolates and 80.6% of the MRSE isolates. Finafloxacin eradicated ciprofloxacin-resistantspp. in 74.4% and ciprofloxacin-resistantspp. in 87.5% of treated patients. Finafloxacin demonstrated high eradication rates in AOE patients with methicillin-resistant.and., as well as in patients with ciprofloxacin-resistantspp.- andspp., irrespective of the pathogen's resistance profile. These in vitro findings, together with observed eradication rates in the vehicle-controlled trials, suggest that finafloxacin may offer advantages in the treatment of resistant organisms, particularly under acidic pH conditions. However, direct clinical trial comparisons have not been conducted. Clinical trial registry name: ClinicalTrials.gov. URL: https://clinicaltrials.gov/. Identifier: NCT01535599 and NCT01535560.

title: Eco-friendly biosynthesis of silver nanoparticles by saprophytic Fusarium solani as a sustainable therapeutic approach for the management of methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus wound infections
abstract: The rising prevalence of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) has prompted the exploration of novel, naturally sourced therapeutic alternatives. Here, the saprophytic fungus Fusarium solani was used to biosynthesize silver nanoparticles (AgNPs), which were characterized by UV-visible spectroscopy, transmission electron microscopy (TEM), scanning electron microscopy (SEM), X-ray diffraction (XRD), and Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR). The AgNPs showed a surface plasmon resonance peak at ~ 410 nm, a zeta potential of - 42.7 mV, an average TEM diameter of 19.58 nm, and a hydrodynamic (DLS) diameter of 121.4 nm with a polydispersity index of 0.302. Against clinical methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) isolates, the AgNPs exhibited minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) and minimum bactericidal concentration (MBC) values of 0.1875-0.375 mM, with confocal laser scanning microscopy (CLSM) showing a reduction in bacterial viability from 92.3% to 28.0% and TEM revealing marked ultrastructural membrane damage following treatment. In a murine MRSA wound infection model, AgNPs treatment increased wound healing from 12.33% to 95.33% and reduced bacterial load from 9.90 to 1.10 log CFU/g tissue relative to the untreated infected control, alongside significant downregulation of TNF-α, IL-6, and COX-2 expression and improved histopathological indices of tissue repair (all p < 0.05). These findings indicate that fungal-derived AgNPs possess potent antibacterial and wound-healing properties against MRSA, supporting their potential as a sustainable therapeutic candidate, although further mechanistic and translational studies are needed.

title: Repeat antimicrobial susceptibility testing of serial bacterial isolates: clinical utility and diagnostic stewardship
abstract: To synthesize evidence on the interpretation and temporal stability of antimicrobial susceptibility profiles in serial bacterial isolates and to identify factors that inform repeat testing within diagnostic stewardship. This narrative review integrates evidence from studies of serial clinical isolates with data on analytical variability, within-host resistance evolution, heteroresistance, antimicrobial exposure, and diagnostic stewardship. Susceptibility profiles are generally stable over short intervals, although clinically relevant changes vary according to bacterial species, antimicrobial agent, specimen context, and elapsed time. Small MIC shifts, particularly near clinical breakpoints, may result in categorical discordance without indicating true resistance emergence. Pseudomonas aeruginosa exhibits greater short-term phenotypic variability than several other common pathogens. Repeat AST is most strongly supported when infection persists or recurs, the clinical response is inadequate, antimicrobial exposure may have selected for resistance, or the consequences of missed resistance are substantial. In selected lower-risk settings, referral to a recent susceptibility result may be appropriate, provided that laboratory and clinical override mechanisms remain available. Short-term susceptibility stability may support conservative referral to a recent AST result, but the degree of instability varies by organism, antimicrobial agent, and specimen context. Where a single operational interval is required, laboratories may adopt the shortest interval supported by local or otherwise applicable evidence, with predefined overrides for higher-risk clinical situations. Prospective multicentre validation is required before specific intervals can be generalized across clinical and laboratory settings.

title: Quorum Sensing and Quenching as Integrated Strategies for Antimicrobial Resistance Mitigation in Aquaculture: Applications and Future Directions
abstract: The rapid expansion of aquaculture has been accompanied by an increased prevalence of bacterial diseases, leading to widespread antibiotic use and the accelerated emergence of antimicrobial resistance (AMR). Rising water temperatures and environmental stressors further exacerbate pathogen proliferation and disease outbreaks, posing significant threats to global aquaculture productivity and sustainability. Quorum sensing (QS), a bacterial cell-to-cell communication system, plays a central role in regulating virulence factor expression, biofilm formation, and AMR-related pathways in aquatic pathogens. Consequently, disrupting QS through quorum quenching (QQ) has emerged as a promising alternative to conventional antibiotic-based treatments. This review synthesizes current knowledge on the mechanisms underlying QS and its role in AMR development in aquaculture systems. It highlights various QQ strategies, including enzymatic degradation of signaling molecules, competitive inhibition using small-molecule quorum sensing inhibitors, and the application of probiotic organisms capable of interfering with QS pathways. Evidence from recent studies demonstrates that QQ can effectively reduce virulence, enhance antibiotic sensitivity, and lower the required dosage of antimicrobial agents. Despite its potential, the implementation of QQ in aquaculture faces several challenges, including environmental stability, scalability, species-specific variability in QS systems, and regulatory concerns. Future research should focus on developing broad-spectrum, non-toxic, and environmentally stable QQ agents, as well as improving delivery systems for practical field applications. Overall, quorum quenching represents a promising, eco-friendly strategy to mitigate AMR, reduce antibiotic dependence, and enhance the sustainability of aquaculture systems worldwide.

title: Biofilm-Mediated pathogenesis in staphylococcal bovine mastitis: A mechanistic review of virulence, pharmacokinetic barriers, and advanced anti-biofilm therapeutic strategies
abstract: Bovine mastitis remains one of the most economically significant infectious diseases affecting dairy production worldwide, causing substantial losses through reduced milk yield, treatment costs, and premature culling. Among the causative agents, Staphylococcus aureus and non-aureus staphylococci (NAS) are particularly problematic due to their capacity to establish chronic intramammary infections through biofilm formation, facilitating immune evasion and marked antimicrobial tolerance. Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, this systematic review integrates mechanistic and translational evidence on biofilm-mediated pathogenesis, pharmacokinetic barriers, and anti-biofilm interventions in staphylococcal bovine mastitis. A structured literature search of PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and Web of Science Core Collection was conducted for investigations published between January 2015 and February 2026. From 513 identified records, 26 primary empirical studies met all eligibility criteria and were synthesized. Mechanistically, staphylococcal biofilm development entails initial adhesion mediated by microbial surface components recognizing adhesive matrix molecules (MSCRAMMs), followed by extracellular matrix accumulation governed by the icaADBC operon responsible for polysaccharide intercellular adhesin (PIA/PNAG) synthesis, alongside ica-independent pathways orchestrated by the biofilm-associated protein (Bap) and extracellular DNA (eDNA). These developmental stages and dispersal dynamics are coordinated by the agr quorum-sensing system and the global regulator sarA. Comparative genomic evidence indicates that NAS species, particularly Staphylococcus chromogenes and Staphylococcus haemolyticus, harbor specialized virulence and antimicrobial resistance determinants that drive subclinical persistence. Beyond bacterial determinants, antimicrobial efficacy is severely constrained by mammary pharmacokinetic barriers, including non-specific drug binding to milk proteins, sequestration in fat globules, and rapid clearance during milking cycles. Emerging therapeutic strategies notably phytochemical-loaded nanoemulsions, matrix-dispersing enzymes, and bacteriophage endolysins-demonstrate substantial capacity to dismantle established biofilms and restore antimicrobial susceptibility in preclinical models. Overcoming persistent staphylococcal mastitis will require translating dual-action formulations combining matrix-degrading agents with advanced delivery systems into validated intramammary therapeutics.

title: Engineering Vibrio natriegens for biopesticide production: from pathway optimization to plant protection
abstract: Phytopathogens pose a persistent threat to global crop production, necessitating the development of sustainable biocontrol strategies. Microbial biopesticides offer a promising alternative to chemical pesticides; however, their industrial application is frequently constrained by low production titers and high substrate costs. This study reprograms the phenazine-1-carboxylic acid (PCA) biosynthetic pathway in Vibrio natriegens, a fast-growing marine bacterium with broad carbon utilization capability. A modular plasmid toolbox is constructed through systematic optimization of promoters, ribosome binding sites, replication origins, and antibiotic resistance markers, enabling high-level PCA production. To address plasmid instability and antibiotic dependence, an I-SceI-based genome editing platform is established, facilitating scarless, multi-copy chromosomal integration of the PCA gene cluster. The final engineered strain, Vna6, achieves PCA titers of 102.0 mg/L in shake flasks and 579.8 mg/L in fed-batch fermentation with glucose as the carbon source. Furthermore, Vna6 exhibits broad-spectrum antagonistic activity against both bacterial (Streptomyces scabies) and fungal (Glomerella cingulata) phytopathogens, as confirmed by in vitro inhibition zone assays and in vivo plant protection experiments on Arabidopsis thaliana and radish seedlings. This work establishes V. natriegens as a potenial chassis for biopesticide production and offers a promising strategy for sustainable crop disease management.

title: Bats, wild rodents, and marsupials as ecosentinels of antimicrobial resistance: a systematized narrative review of resistance genes, mobile genetic elements, and One Health implications
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a major One Health challenge, yet wildlife remains underrepresented in surveillance systems. This systematized narrative review synthesized studies published between 2011 and 2025 on antimicrobial-resistant bacteria in bats, wild rodents, and marsupials, aiming to evaluate their role as reservoirs, disseminators, and ecosentinels of environmental AMR. The search was conducted in PubMed, SciELO, MEDLINE, and Scopus, and original studies reporting bacterial identification and phenotypic or genotypic resistance data were included. A total of 110 studies met the inclusion criteria, comprising rodents (n = 56), bats (n = 37), and marsupials (n = 17). The most frequently reported bacterial groups included Escherichia coli, Staphylococcus spp., Klebsiella pneumoniae, Enterococcus spp., and Salmonella spp. Rodents frequently harbored multidrug-resistant Enterobacterales, including ESBL-producing E. coli and resistance genes associated with last-line antimicrobials, reflecting exposure to urban, agricultural, and waste-contaminated environments. Bats were prominent reservoirs of resistant Staphylococcus spp., including methicillin-resistant strains, and carried clinically relevant Gram-negative bacteria, likely influenced by mobility, diet, colony behavior, and anthropogenic landscape exposure. Marsupials generally showed lower AMR burdens in free-ranging conditions, but captive and rehabilitated individuals exhibited increased resistance, suggesting human-mediated acquisition and amplification. Across host groups, the detection of mobile genetic elements and resistance determinants shared with clinical contexts supports the occurrence of cross-ecosystem exchange. These findings reinforce the need to integrate wildlife into AMR monitoring frameworks as early-warning indicators of environmental contamination and resistance dissemination.

title: Microalgae-based removal and biodegradation of antibiotics: mechanisms, synergistic consortia, and engineering prospects
abstract: Antibiotic pollution in aquatic environments drives the spread of resistance genes and threatens ecosystem health. Microalgae offer a dual-function platform that both senses antibiotic stress and actively removes these contaminants. This review synthesizes current knowledge on microalgae-based antibiotic removal and biotransformation, emphasizing the integration of biosorption, enzyme-mediated transformation-primarily via cytochrome P450 and nitroreductase-and co‑metabolic processes. We highlight the phycosphere as a dynamic interface where symbiotic bacteria enhance algal survival and pollutant removal, while also modulating the enrichment and dissemination of resistance genes. Algal-bacterial granular sludge systems illustrate the practical potential of this synergy, achieving efficient antibiotic removal and suppression of resistance propagation. Emerging tools such as immobilization, synthetic biology, and machine learning show potential to further improve system robustness and may facilitate precision process control, although their scalability and long-term performance remain to be validated. By linking fundamental mechanisms with engineering strategies, this review provides a framework for developing sustainable, low-carbon bioremediation technologies aligned with global antimicrobial resistance action plans.

title: Genomic and functional characterisation of exopolysaccharide biosynthesis in marine bacterium Alteromonas sp. PRIM-28 with emulsifying and anti-inflammatory activities
abstract: Bacterial exopolysaccharides (EPS) are structurally heterogeneous biopolymers governed by species- and strain-specific biosynthetic pathways and with diverse biotechnological applications. The study investigated EPS biosynthesis in a marine bacterium, Alteromonas sp. PRIM-28 through an integrated genomic and experimental approach. Whole-genome sequencing and functional annotation were performed to identify the gene clusters and regulatory elements associated with EPS biosynthesis. The salt tolerance of the bacterium was studied at salt concentrations of up to 25%. EPS production was assessed using the ethanol precipitation method and partial characterisation, including emulsification and anti-inflammatory assays. Draft genome contained 3444 coding sequences with 97.6% completeness. Phylogenetic and ANI analyses confirmed its close relation to Alteromonas fortis (96.2%). Genome mining identified wzy-dependent and generic-cellulose EPS biosynthesis clusters along with the presence of epsCDEFHLM genes. CAZyme and KEGG analysis revealed diverse carbohydrate-active enzymes and complete central carbohydrate metabolism pathways, supporting EPS biosynthesis in PRIM-28. Presence of saline and oxidative stress-tolerance genes (nqrABCDEF, opuED, sglTSBC and katABEG) suggest bacterium's environmental adaptability. Genes associated with virulence factors and antimicrobial resistance were not identified supporting the suitability of the strain for industrial use. The strain tolerated salinity up to 15%. The highest EPS production was seen at 96 h (2.40 ± 0.09 g L). The EPS contained ~ 60% total sugars, showed emulsification activity against different oils, and exhibited anti-inflammatory activity in the albumin denaturation assay (80.7 ± 0.9%) comparable to positive control (p > 0.05). The combined genomic and functional evidence establishes the EPS biosynthesis in PRIM-28 and highlight its potential as a sustainable biopolymer source.

title: Genomic Characterization of Multidrug-Resistant Enterobacter hormaechei from Bovine Raw Milk: Implications for Food Safety and Public Health
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance in foodborne bacteria poses a growing threat to public health. In this study, multidrug-resistant Enterobacter hormaechei (E. hormaechei), a member of the Enterobacter cloacae complex (ECC), was isolated from bovine raw milk in Gujarat, India, and examined for its prevalence, antimicrobial resistance, and genomic characteristics. A total of 21 presumptive E. hormaechei isolates were recovered from 190 raw milk samples (11.05%) based on morphological and biochemical characteristics and further confirmed using a species-specific PCR assay. Based on their phenotypic antimicrobial resistance profiles, eight multidrug-resistant (MDR) isolates were selected for whole-genome sequencing and downstream genomic analyses. Whole-genome sequencing of the MDR isolates revealed distinct sequence types, with ST350 and ST68 clustered closely. The sequenced isolates harbored a diverse repertoire of antimicrobial resistance genes, including blaACT, qnrS1/qnrB7, fosA, oqxA/B, mph(A), and aminoglycoside-modifying enzymes, consistent with their multidrug-resistant phenotypes. Virulence profiling identified genes associated with iron acquisition, adhesion, stress response, and type VI secretion systems, suggesting the presence of virulence-associated genetic determinants. Plasmid replicons (IncFII and Col-type) and the insertion sequence IS26 were identified among the sequenced isolates. This study provides a genomic characterization of MDR E. hormaechei isolates from raw milk in Gujarat, India, and emphasizes the importance of continuous AMR surveillance to monitor the spread of Enterobacter lineages with relevance to food safety and public health.

title: From Spore Biology to System Performance: Strain-Resolved Mechanisms, Biosafety and Translational Readiness of Bacillus Probiotics in Aquaculture
abstract: Bacillus-based probiotics are widely promoted as antibiotic-sparing interventions in aquaculture, yet translation from controlled trials to commercial production remains constrained by strain heterogeneity, inconsistent dosing, incomplete biosafety assessment and frequent inference of mechanisms from non-specific biomarkers. This scoping review reorganizes the evidence reported for 67 empirical studies published during 2015-2025 into a strain-host-route-system framework. Across finfish and aquatic invertebrates, Bacillus supplementation was commonly associated with improved growth, feed utilization, digestive-enzyme activity, mucosal or systemic innate immune indices, challenge survival and, in water-applied or biofloc settings, nitrogenous-waste control. The evidence nevertheless does not support a universal optimal dose: reported regimens span colony-forming units per gram or kilogram of feed, colony-forming units per millilitre of culture water and mass-based commercial formulations, and efficacy varies with strain identity, host developmental stage, delivery route, diet, salinity, temperature and challenge design. Mechanistic support is strongest for pathogen antagonism, enzyme provision, barrier modulation and environmental bioremediation, whereas claims concerning stable colonization, antiviral action and antimicrobial-resistance mitigation are often indirect. Bacillus should therefore be evaluated at strain rather than genus level, with whole-genome screening for virulence determinants, toxins, transferable resistance genes and mobile elements. We propose a translational-readiness framework integrating identity, potency, formulation stability, host compatibility, environmental persistence, biosafety and farm-scale validation. This reframing positions Bacillus probiotics as promising but conditional tools for antibiotic stewardship and One Health-aligned aquaculture.

title: Lipid Extract from Ulva ohnoi Algae: Chemical Characterization, Antibacterial Potential, and Cytotoxicity in the Search for New Agents Against MDR Infections
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance is a critical global concern. This study explored the lipid extract (LE) of Ulva ohnoi regarding its chemical composition, antibacterial activity, and cytotoxicity against multidrug-resistant (MDR) microorganisms. The LE was characterized by GC-MS, thermogravimetric analysis (TGA), and differential scanning calorimetry (DSC). Antibacterial efficacy was determined by Minimum Inhibitory Concentration (MIC) and Minimum Bactericidal Concentration (MBC) against MDR isolates: Acinetobacter baumannii, Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Staphylococcus aureus, and coagulase-negative Staphylococci (CoNS). Cytotoxicity was evaluated in murine fibroblast (L929) and bovine renal fibroblast (MDBK) cells using MTT, Neutral Red (NR), Lactate Dehydrogenase (LDH), and hemolytic activity (HA) assays. Lipid characterization revealed palmitic acid (63.62%) and oleic acid (21.01%) as major components. TGA indicated 88% mass loss, and DSC showed no amorphous/crystalline domains. LE showed favorable MIC values against S. aureus and CoNS (1.33 mg/mL) and against A. baumannii and E. coli (2 mg/mL), indicating moderate antibacterial activity typical of an unfractionated crude extract. MBC results indicated bacteriostatic activity (1-8 mg/mL). The extract was cytotoxic to L929 and MDBK cells at concentrations close to its MIC (IC₅₀ 0.25-1.95 mg/mL) but well tolerated by blood cells (HA IC4.705 mg/mL). U. ohnoi LE extends, rather than establishes, the previously reported antibacterial potential of Ulva lipids through comprehensive chemical characterization and MDR-isolate evaluation. However, low selectivity indices (SI < 10) indicate that the LE does not yet present an adequate therapeutic window, reinforcing the need for bioassay-guided purification. Nevertheless, it is a starting point for developing new antibacterial agents.

title: Combined antibacterial and antibiofilm activity of an Ag-CeO₂/MgAl-LDH nanocomposite-nanoemulsion formulation against multidrug-resistant Enterococcus faecium
abstract: The increasing prevalence of multidrug-resistant (MDR) Enterococcus faecium has created an urgent need for alternative antimicrobial strategies capable of overcoming conventional antibiotic resistance and inhibiting biofilm formation. In the present study, the antibacterial and antibiofilm activities of an Ag-CeO₂/MgAl-LDH nanocomposite, a sunflower oil-based nanoemulsion, and their combined formulation were evaluated against both a clinical MDR isolate and the reference strain E. faecium MCC 2763. The prepared formulations were characterized using dynamic light scattering (DLS), zeta potential analysis, and Fourier transform infrared (FTIR) spectroscopy. Antibacterial activity was assessed by minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC), minimum bactericidal concentration (MBC), time-kill kinetics, impedance-based growth monitoring, bacterial adherence assays, and biofilm inhibition studies. The combined nanocomposite-nanoemulsion formulation showed greater antibacterial and antibiofilm activity than the individual formulations under the experimental conditions evaluated. Time-kill and biofilm assays indicated improved inhibition of bacterial growth and biofilm formation, while impedance measurements further supported the antibacterial activity of the combined formulation. Although the present findings demonstrate the promising antibacterial potential of the developed formulation, formal synergy analysis, cytotoxicity evaluation, advanced physicochemical characterization, and mechanistic investigations were beyond the scope of this study. These investigations will be essential in future work to further evaluate the therapeutic potential of this formulation. Overall, the developed Ag-CeO₂/MgAl-LDH nanocomposite-nanoemulsion formulation represents a promising antibacterial platform for combating multidrug-resistant Enterococcus faecium and warrants further investigation through comprehensive preclinical evaluation.

title: Addressing threats to future global health-what is the right timeframe?
Identification of atypical Escherichia coli as hidden reservoir of tet(X4)-positive IncX1 plasmid
abstract: The horizontal dissemination of antimicrobial resistance genes (ARGs) poses a significant threat to public health. In this study, we investigated the presence and transferability of a tet(X4)-positive IncX1 plasmid in an atypical Escherichia coli isolate, GX-3-49. Genomic analysis revealed that GX-3-49 is markedly distinct from conventional E. coli, characterized by a reduced gene repertoire, fewer toxin genes, and a distinct phylogenetic lineage. Phenotypic characterization further demonstrated that, compared to the reference strain EC25922, GX-3-49 exhibits diminished motility, growth, and virulence, alongside a marked increase in biofilm formation and pH tolerance , but greater sensitivity to high temperature. These findings suggested that GX-3-49 might have evolved a fitness trade-off, reducing its virulence in exchange for enhanced resilience under acidic and biofilm-forming conditions. Additionally, a tet(X4)-positive IncX1 plasmid co-harboring bla, tet(A), and floR, were identified in GX-3-49 and remained stable during serial passaging. This plasmid exhibited high sequence similarity to IncX1 plasmids previously identified in E. coli and Klebsiella pneumoniae and was capable of conjugative transfer to E. coli EC600, suggesting its potential for interspecies dissemination. In conclusion, this study identified a stable and transferable tet(X4)-positive IncX1 plasmid in an atypical E. coli strain exhibiting reduced virulence and increased susceptibility to heat, yet enhanced stress resilience under specific environmental conditions. These findings highlight the potential of such bacteria to serve as hidden reservoirs for antimicrobial resistance and facilitate the dissemination of ARGs.

title: Molecular epidemiology of NDM-producing Enterobacterales in Huai'an, China: Genomic diversity and evaluation of aztreonam-avibactam and cefiderocol
abstract: Metallo-β-lactamase-producing carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales (MBL-CRE) pose a serious threat due to antimicrobial resistance. However, their prevalence in the Huai'an region of Jiangsu Province in eastern China remains unknown. Carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales (CRE) isolates collected from Xuyi People's Hospital were screened for carbapenemase production using the modified carbapenem inactivation method (mCIM) and EDTA-modified carbapenem inactivation method (eCIM), followed by PCR confirmation. Antimicrobial susceptibility testing, biofilm formation assays, growth kinetics analyses, and whole-genome sequencing with bioinformatics were performed to characterize the isolates. The 12 NDM-producing Enterobacterales identified comprised seven Escherichia coli, three Klebsiella pneumoniae, and two Enterobacter hormaechei. Beyond carbapenem resistance, resistance to aztreonam, tetracycline, fluoroquinolones, and aminoglycosides was common among the isolates. Four isolates (including three E. coli) showed intermediate susceptibility to cefiderocol, and the aztreonam-avibactam combination exhibited synergistic activity against aztreonam-resistant Enterobacteriaceae isolates. Genomic analysis revealed eight isolates carrying bla, three carrying bla, and one carrying bla. All isolates belonged to distinct sequence types, including two novel types. The NDM-13 isolate and one NDM-1-positive E. hormaechei isolate displayed distinct genetic contexts, whereas most isolates harbored a bla-ble-trpF-tat-dct genetic structure. Among the three cefiderocol-intermediate E. coli isolates, mutations were identified in cirA and ftsI. This study reveals the prevalence and diverse genetic backgrounds of MBL-CRE in Xuyi County, demonstrates the potent activity of aztreonam-avibactam, and suggests that cefiderocol resistance may involve multiple factors.

title: Facilitating non-radical peroxymonosulfate oxidation of tetracyclines driven by struvite crystallization
abstract: Eliminating residual antibiotics during struvite recovery from livestock wastewater is essential to prevent the spread of antibiotic resistance. In this work, the effects of in-situ struvite crystallization on the degradation of typical veterinary antibiotics, tetracyclines (TCs), by non-radical peroxymonosulfate (PMS) oxidation were investigated. Results revealed that the process of struvite crystallization enhanced PMS oxidation of TCs with kvalues reaching 1.95-2.15 times those of PMS alone.Oand electron transfer processes were identified as the dominant non-radical pathways. Electrochemical analyses indicated that electron transfer processes would be more active through crystallization than pre-formed crystals in PMS oxidation due to the higher interfacial reactivity. Mg:P molar ratio and pH affected TCs degradation through regulating struvite crystallization and altering the speciation of TCs and PMS, with Mg:P ratio of 1.0 and pH 9.2-9.8 being optimal for facilitatingOgeneration and PMS oxidation. In the presence of humic acid (HA), HA-TCs complexes caused an inhibitory effect on TCs degradation, and excess Mgmitigated this inhibition by reducing the direct association between TCs and HA. Fourier transform ion cyclotron resonance mass spectrometry (FT-ICR-MS) and fluorescence spectroscopy analyses revealed that HA underwent selective molecular restructuring, with nitrogen-containing and highly condensed aromatic components being converted into more oxygenated and less aromatic products through oxygenation, which could further favor electron transfer pathways. This study highlights that struvite crystallization enhances non-radical oxidation and provides new insights into antibiotic removal with simultaneous phosphorus recovery in livestock wastewater.

title: Salmonellosis outbreaks associated with pork, United States, 2012-2021
abstract: Nontyphoidal Salmonella causes an estimated 1.3 million domestically-acquired foodborne infections in humans annually in the United States (Scallan Walter et al., 2025). From 1998 to 2023, pork was the fourth most common food category attributed to foodborne Salmonella illnesses (Interagency Food Safety Analytics Collaboration, 2024). We analyzed salmonellosis outbreaks associated with pork products between 2012-2021, using data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention's Foodborne Diseases Outbreak Surveillance System, System for Enteric Disease Response, Investigation, and Coordination, PulseNet, and the National Antimicrobial Resistance Monitoring System. There were 50 Salmonella outbreaks linked to pork from 2012-2021. Twenty-one different Salmonella serotypes were identified; serotype I 4,[5],12:i:- was the most common, causing 19/50 outbreaks, followed by Typhimurium (7/50). Raw ground pork was associated with three outbreaks (6%) and 444 illnesses (23%). Pork roast or shoulder was associated with 13 outbreaks (26%) and 408 illnesses (21%). Whole pigs were associated with 11 outbreaks (22%) and 368 illnesses (19%). Among Salmonella isolates with available antimicrobial resistance information, 226/389 (58%) showed multidrug resistance and 230/389 (59%) showed clinically significant resistance; 216/222 (97%) and 22/34 (65%) of I 4,[5],12:i:- and Typhimurium isolates, respectively, exhibited any resistance. Antimicrobial resistance in Salmonella isolates from outbreaks linked to pork was more frequent than for nontyphoidal Salmonella infections in the United States overall. Preharvest disease prevention efforts that target serotypes I 4,[5],12:i:- and Typhimurium may be valuable in reducing Salmonella outbreaks and illnesses. Downstream exploration of individual- and community-level factors related to handling, preparation, and consumption of specific pork types may help reduce salmonellosis rates through targeted education.

title: Global phylogenomic structure and accessory resistance dynamics of Acinetobacter baumannii ST2
abstract: Acinetobacter baumannii sequence type 2 (Pasteur ST2), associated with international clone 2, is a major antimicrobial-resistant lineage, but its within-lineage population structure and accessory resistance variation remain incompletely resolved. We analyzed 5612 quality-filtered public genomes from an existing global dataset using PopPUNK, core-genome SNP analysis, AMRFinderPlus, MobileElementFinder and MOB-suite. A dominant PopPUNK cluster contained 5604 genomes (99.86%). Its SNP phylogeny showed dense short-distance relationships within a connected lineage; pairwise distances had a median of 314 SNPs. Four antibiotic classes-beta-lactams, aminoglycosides, phenicols and fosfomycin-were detected in at least 95% of dominant-cluster genomes. The median antibiotic-class annotation hit count was 14 per genome (IQR, 13-15), including intrinsic and lineage-associated determinants. Predicted conjugative and mobilizable plasmid signatures occurred in 52.6% and 42.7% of dominant-cluster genomes, respectively. Across the full cohort, mobile-element and antibiotic-class hit counts were weakly positively correlated (Spearman ρ = 0.191). This unadjusted association was absent among 700 representatives selected one per ≤10-SNP component (ρ = -0.0721; p = 0.0567), and a component-bootstrap interval included zero. Assembly-adjusted associations differed between the full cohort and representatives. The small positive unadjusted collection-year association was not robust to location adjustment and was unsupported in dated representatives. Complete-genome annotations documented both chromosomal and plasmid blacopies and upstream ISAba1 proximity, without establishing promoter activity or resistance phenotype. These findings describe a cohesive ST2 lineage with heterogeneous accessory resistance and plasmid-mobility signatures, while emphasizing the sensitivity of genome-wide associations to assembly characteristics and clonal and geographic sampling.

title: When is travel-health AI inference transportable? Mobility-conditioned admissibility for cross-border disease risk and decision support
abstract: Artificial intelligence is increasingly used for infectious disease surveillance, traveller risk assessment, outbreak forecasting and decision support. Travel creates a distinctive transportability problem because people move between epidemiological, geographic, climatic and healthcare contexts in which the conditions supporting an inference may change rapidly. This conceptual/theoretical methodological-development study was informed by a targeted narrative review of travel medicine, infectious disease surveillance, human mobility, border health, mass gatherings, antimicrobial resistance and health-AI validation literature. We develop a mobility-conditioned admissibility framework that treats travel as movement across origin, transit, destination and return regimes. Interpretation is conditioned on mobility state, epidemiological regime, exposure history, time-dependent constraints and clinical or biological constraints. Five proposed operational states are retained: supported inference, conditionally transportable inference, active monitoring, restricted interpretation and withholding. The framework also distinguishes low probability from infeasibility and requires preservation of rare but epidemiologically feasible events. Model availability and conventional predictive validity do not establish inferential transportability across changing travel contexts. Mobility-conditioned admissibility provides a complementary use-boundary layer for travel health AI by making cross-regime support explicit before outputs are interpreted or released. Its incremental value requires prospective evaluation against calibrated uncertainty, external validation and dataset-shift monitoring.

title: Conjugative IncHI1 plasmids drive the emergence of multidrug resistance in Nigerian Salmonella Typhi: A four-decade genomic analysis
abstract: The role of plasmids in driving antimicrobial resistance (AMR) in West African Salmonella Typhi remains unexplored. This study investigates the prevalence, temporal dynamics, and genetic associations of plasmid mobility classes and replicon types in Nigerian S. typhi over nearly four decades. We analyzed 151 S. typhi genomes from Nigeria (1982-2018) obtained from EnteroBase. Plasmid replicon typing and mobility classification revealed that 49.7% of isolates harbored conjugative plasmids, with the IncHI1 family (IncHI1A, IncHI1B_R27, and IncFIA_HI1) being the most prevalent.
