Fluorinated Aliphatic Thiols in the Design of Cephalosporin Conjugates for Metallo-β-Lactamase Inhibition
abstract: Antibiotic resistance is a major global health challenge, with the rapid spread of metallo-β-lactamase (MBL)-expressing bacteria presenting a serious clinical threat. In this study, we synthesized and investigated a series of novel cephalosporin conjugates envisioned to release MBL inhibitors upon MBL-mediated hydrolysis. The designed compounds consist of a cephalosporin core linked to trifluoromethylated aliphatic thiol-based MBL inhibitors. Conjugates releasing aliphatic thiols upon hydrolysis by the New Delhi Metallo-β-lactamase-1 (NDM-1) were identified, confirming that fluorination improves the leaving group properties of some aliphatic thiols compared to a nonfluorinated control. However, when comparing with a conjugate containing an aromatic thiol, fluorinated aliphatic thiol release appeared slower and mechanistically more complex, thus incompletely resolved. The conjugates exhibited potent inhibitory activity against several subclass B1 MBLs. In addition, the utility ofF NMR as an alternative method for hydrolysis monitoring was exemplified. The findings highlight the potential, but also some unsolved challenges, of altering the leaving group ability of aliphatic thiol-based inhibitors to exploit the catalytic activity of NDM-1 for the selective release of inhibitors in MBL-producing bacteria.

title: Integrated In Silico Analysis Reveals ABC Transporter ATP-Binding Protein as a Therapeutic Target in Helicobacter pylori
abstract: remains a major cause of gastric diseases, while increasing antimicrobial resistance highlights the need for novel therapeutic targets. Here, we developed a comprehensive computational target-prioritization framework integrating Rosetta Stone domain-fusion analysis, subtractive genomics, metabolic pathway mapping, structural modeling, and molecular dynamics simulations to identify pathogen-specific drug targets inJ99. Twelve conserved domain families comprising 746 proteins were identified, and domain abundance showed a weak negative correlation with versatility (= -0.327), suggesting functional specialization through domain expansion. Sequential filtering based on essentiality, nonhomology to the human proteome and gut microbiota, subcellular localization, and druggability prioritized five candidate proteins, with the ATP-binding protein AAD06727.1 emerging as the most promising target. AlphaFold2 modeling produced a high-confidence structure containing a conserved nucleotide-binding pocket. Molecular docking identified 5'-fluorosulfonylbenzoyl-5'-adenosine (FSBA) as the highest-affinity ligand (-7.3 kcal mol), outperforming ATP and verapamil. Triplicate 1 μs molecular dynamics simulations of apo and halo AAD06727.1 demonstrated stable rmsd, RMSF, radius of gyration, solvent-accessible surface area, hydrogen-bond occupancy, and principal component profiles, indicating preservation of structural integrity following ATP binding. Comparative simulations with the human ABCA12 nucleotide-binding domain showed conserved global architecture while revealing distinct ligand-recognition characteristics. Together, these findings identify AAD06727.1 as a structurally stable, pathogen-specific ATP-binding protein that represents a promising candidate for future structure-guided anti-drug development.

title: Adsorption of Levofloxacin onto Chitosan- and Layered Double Hydroxide-Functionalized Montmorillonite
abstract: Antibiotic contamination of water resources is a major environmental concern. Beyond their direct toxicity to nontarget aquatic organisms, antibiotic-contaminated waters can serve as reservoirs for the development of antimicrobial resistance (AMR). Levofloxacin (LVX), a third-generation fluoroquinolone antibiotic, has frequently been detected in various environmental media. In this study, the LVX adsorption performance of chitosan/montmorillonite (CTS/MMT) and CO-type MgAl layered double hydroxide/montmorillonite (LDH/MMT) composites was evaluated in batch experiments. MMT, a naturally occurring phyllosilicate clay, was functionalized with either the polysaccharide CTS or the anionic clay LDH. The synthesized CTS/MMT composite maintained a negative surface charge across the whole pH range from 2.0 to 12.0, whereas LDH/MMT exhibited an isoelectric point (IEP) at pH 5.1. Key operational parameters, including solution pH, contact time, temperature, and initial LVX concentration, were then optimized. Both adsorbents showed maximum adsorption at pH 3 in a 30 mg LLVX solution after 60 min, with removal efficiencies of 77.7% and 99.1% for 0.01 g of LDH/MMT and CTS/MMT, respectively. Temperature variation data showed that LVX adsorption efficiency for LDH/MMT remained largely unaffected, ∼78.0% for a 0.01 g dosage, ∼90.0% for 0.05 g, and ∼87.0% for 0.1 g throughout the temperature range 15-35 °C. In contrast, CTS/MMT consistently achieved near-complete LVX removal (∼100.0%) across all tested temperatures regardless of dosage. For 0.01 g of adsorbent dosage, CTS/MMT adsorbed >99.0% LVX within 60 min, whereas adsorption onto LDH/MMT achieved equilibrium within 10 min with 77.1% removal efficiency. The Langmuir model fitted the CTS/MMT adsorption data well, with a maximum adsorption capacity of 107.53 mg g, whereas the Freundlich model better described the adsorption behavior of LDH/MMT. For CTS/MMT, at pH < 5.59, surface adsorption through electrostatic attraction between cationic LVX and the negatively charged composite surface, coupled with cation exchange into the MMT interlayer, may be the principal adsorption phenomenon. On the other hand, heterogeneous intercalation of cationic LVX molecules into the MMT interlayer was the principal mechanism for LVX adsorption onto LDH/MMT.

title: Evaluation of the BioFire joint infection panel in Taiwan: Impact of regional non-target pathogens and joint type on its performance
abstract: The BIOFIRE® Joint Infection (BJI) panel, a rapid multiplex polymerase chain reaction assay, is used to diagnose joint infections. Here we used it to evaluate the clinical performance and impact of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) detection in Taiwan's unique microbial landscape. Adult patients with suspected septic arthritis or prosthetic joint infection were prospectively enrolled from four hospitals in southern Taiwan. Synovial fluid specimens were tested using a BJI panel and routine bacterial culturing. Performance was assessed by calculating the positive percent agreement and negative percent agreement (PPA and NPA, respectively). Eighty-six specimens (native joints, 56; prosthetic joints, 30) were analyzed. The overall PPA and NPA were 92.3% and 76.7%, respectively. Native joints showed higher concordance (PPA, 93.8%; NPA, 85.0%) than prosthetic joints (PPA, 90.0%; NPA, 60.0%). The BJI panel detected pathogens in 14 culture-negative cases, predominantly among patients who previously received antibiotics. Notably, the panel identified six methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus cases (three culture-negative) and one bla-positive E. coli detection. However, three culture-positive cases involving "off-panel" regional pathogens (Burkholderia pseudomallei, n = 2; Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex, n = 1) were BJI-negative. Diagnostic concordance is better in native joints and correlated significantly with higher synovial leukocyte counts. Our evaluation revealed the BJI panel's ability to rapidly identify pathogens and profile AMR, with additional diagnostic yield particularly in culture-negative prosthetic joint infections and in patients with prior antibiotic exposure. However, its limited detection targets leave a diagnostic gap for regionally endemic pathogens such as Burkholderia pseudomallei and Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex, indicating the continued need for conventional culturing.

title: Assessment of antibiotic residues and microbiological safety in Lebanese dairy products: Akkawi cheese, yogurt, and labneh, collected across Lebanese dairy industries
abstract: Antibiotic residues in dairy products and the resulting antibiotic-resistant bacteria represent a major global public health concern. This study evaluated the microbiological safety of 400 dairy samples collected over two consecutive years (2022 and 2023) from 16 dairy residue industries across four governorates in Lebanon. In addition, antibiotic residues were screened from 126 dairy product samples randomly chosen out of the 400. An optimized multi-class method for the identification and quantification of 30 antibiotics was developed using liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry. Results revealed that 48% of the analyzed samples were contaminated with at least one antibiotic residue, among which 33% showed co-occurrence of multiple antibiotic classes. Meanwhile, microbiological assessment of 400 dairy samples collected over 2 years from the same dairies revealed higher levels of contamination with total coliforms, Escherichia coli, and Staphylococcus aureus in Akkawi cheese samples collected during the first year (44%, 32%, and 15%, respectively) compared to those collected the second year (38.8%, 31%, and 0%). Moderate contamination levels were observed in Labneh (strained yogurt) samples collected during both seasons, with yeast (12%; 11%), molds (1.2%; 11%), total coliforms (6%; 11%), and Escherichia coli (3.7%; 11%). On the other hand, comparable levels of non-conformity were observed in yogurt samples across the two years, with contamination by yeast (7.5%; 6.2%), molds (3.75%; 6.2%), total coliforms (26%; 31.2%), E. coli (20%; 21%), and Staphylococcus aureus (1.25%; 0%). Escherichia coli isolates exhibited resistance to tetracycline while being 100% sensitive to ciprofloxacin and nalidixic acid. As for S. aureus isolates, they presented a high sensitivity to tetracyclines, doxycycline, and ciprofloxacin. These findings highlight the importance of implementing and maintaining good hygienic practices within dairy industries. Antimicrobial residues of oxytetracycline, tetracycline, ciprofloxacin, sulfamethazine, and doxycycline were detected at levels below the maximum residue limits.
